question.text: Is the Androgen Deficiency of Aging Men (ADAM) questionnaire useful for the screening of partial androgenic deficiency of aging men?
question.context: Androgen serum levels significantly decrease in older men, causing quality of life impairment and increasing the risk of chronic disease. This disorder is defined as PADAM (Partial Androgen Deficiency of Aging Men). To evaluate a PADAM screening tool and determine the prevalence of this disorder in healthy adult men. This was a cross-sectional study in which 96 men aged 40 or more of the South Metropolitan Region of Santiago de Chile were surveyed with the Androgen Deficiency of Aging Men (ADAM) questionnaire of the Saint Louis University and sampled for the serum determination of total testosterone, sexual hormone binding globulin (SHBG) and albumin. Also free and bioavailable testosterone were calculated. PADAM was considered present if items 1 or 7 or any 3 other questions of the ADAM questionnaire were positive. An available testosterone of<198.4 ng/dL was used as a gold standard for the diagnosis of PADAM. A total of 78 men (81.3%) were identified as possible PADAM according to the ADAM questionnaire. Total testosterone levels fell from 503.6+/-180.1 ng/dL in men aged 40 to 54 years to 382.1+/-247.3 in those>70 years; however this was not statistically significant (ANOVA, p=0.06). In the same age groups, SHBG significantly increased (31.0+/-15.0 to 47.5+/-15.0 nmol/L, p<0.001) whereas free and available testosterone significantly decreased (10.6+/-3.2 to 6.4+/-3.6 ng/dL and 266.6+/-81.2 to 152.2+/-97.6 ng/dL, respectively, p<0.0001). Overall (n=96), available testosterone confirmed PADAM diagnosis in 27 cases (28.1%). The ADAM tool rendered a 83.3% sensitivity and 19.7% specificity in the detection of PADAM. Item 1 (decreased sexual desire) was a better predictor of hypogonadism than the complete questionnaire (63.3% sensitivity and 66.7% specificity).

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The ADAM questionnaire, when combined with serum testosterone levels, appears to be a useful screening tool for PADAM in older men. The study found that 78% of men screened positive for PADAM based on the questionnaire, and 28% were confirmed by available testosterone levels. While the sensitivity and specificity of the questionnaire are not ideal, the study suggests it can be a helpful initial screening tool.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: The ADAM questionnaire rendered a 83.3% sensitivity and 19.7% specificity in the detection of PADAM.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: Other potential screening tools for hypogonadism exist, but the ADAM questionnaire is specifically designed for older men and has been validated in this population. Other conditions that can cause similar symptoms to PADAM, such as depression or other medical conditions, were not specifically addressed in the study.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The ADAM questionnaire showed only 28.1% sensitivity and 19.7% specificity in detecting PADAM, with item 1 (decreased sexual desire) having better predictive value (63.3% sensitivity, 66.7% specificity). The study found no statistically significant difference in testosterone levels across age groups (p=0.06), and only 27 of 78 men (34.6%) with positive ADAM scores had confirmed low available testosterone, indicating poor diagnostic accuracy.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: The ADAM questionnaire's 28.1% sensitivity and 19.7% specificity in detecting PADAM, with no statistically significant testosterone decline across age groups (p=0.06), demonstrates its limited diagnostic value.
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: While age-related hormonal changes are common, the study's findings suggest that the ADAM questionnaire may not reliably distinguish true PADAM from normal age-related changes, making it less useful for screening than direct hormonal testing.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The ADAM questionnaire demonstrated very low specificity (19.7%) and moderate sensitivity (83.3%) for detecting PADAM, indicating it is not reliable for screening due to high false-positive rates. Item 1 alone was a better predictor than the full questionnaire, suggesting the tool lacks robust diagnostic accuracy.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: The ADAM tool had only 19.7% specificity, meaning it incorrectly identified most non-PADAM men as having the condition, making it unsuitable for screening.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Other androgen deficiency screening tools (e.g., based on free testosterone) were not evaluated, but the low specificity of ADAM rules out its use as a primary screening instrument.

Even though sensitivity is moderate, the clinical utility of a screening tool is compromised when specificity is this poor, as it would lead to unnecessary testing and treatment in most men.
